scores.evidence: Merge the two result lists with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), then reorder the top results with a reranking model.
scores.rationale: Technical claims (hybrid search, RRF, pgvector adequacy at this scale, prompt caching, citation validation, the Air Canada precedent) are accurate and the plan states real limits, e.g. deflection measurement caveats.

scores.evidence: Version 1 answers questions from the docs only. It can't look up or change customer accounts.
scores.rationale: Fits the request precisely, resolves ambiguities with stated assumptions and explicit scope exclusions (community posts, account access), weighs build-vs-buy, and is clearly buildable by 1–2 engineers.

scores.evidence: generate (mid-tier LLM, streamed, cites doc ids) ... After the answer is complete, check it for promises
scores.rationale: The pipeline is clear and internally consistent with clean data ownership, but the post-completion commitment check conflicts with streaming: users may see a bad answer before it is replaced.

scores.evidence: Run the tests automatically on every change to prompts, models, chunking or embeddings, and block changes that make scores worse.
scores.rationale: Test set is built before the bot exists, retrieval is scored separately, the LLM grader is validated against human labels, deflection uses an A/B control, and validation continues post-launch via weekly reviews.

scores.evidence: 100–5,000 articles on a help-center platform with an API (Zendesk, Intercom, Freshdesk…) or Markdown files in git.
scores.rationale: Assumptions are explicitly listed, estimates are labeled as such, and a 'Questions that would change the plan' section identifies exactly which assumptions the design is sensitive to.

scores.evidence: The nightly check also removes archived or unpublished articles. Old articles left in the index lead to confident wrong answers.
scores.rationale: Stale content, leaked internal docs, injection, fabricated commitments, duplicates and abuse are all handled concretely, but runtime partial failures (LLM/embedding provider outage or degradation) have no stated fallback.

scores.evidence: Keep prompts in version control. For every conversation turn, log the rewritten query, the retrieved IDs and scores, the prompt, index and model versions
scores.rationale: Logging, versioning, ownership (support-ops owner) and phased rollout are concrete and sized to a small team, but deployment/rollback mechanics, alerting and incident response are not spelled out.

scores.evidence: each message uses about 5–10k input tokens and about 300 output tokens. That's a few cents per conversation
scores.rationale: Dominant driver (inference) is estimated with a stated token basis, controls (caching, model tiers, rate limits, spending cap) are concrete, and build-vs-buy with per-resolution vendor pricing is weighed.

Build-vs-buy is examined early, orchestration is kept thin to avoid framework lock-in, and alternatives are listed, but hard-to-reverse items like chunk/citation ID schemes and embedding-model migration are not explicitly flagged.

scores.evidence: You don't need a separate vector database. A help center is only thousands of chunks, so Postgres with the pgvector extension is enough.
scores.rationale: Starts with the simplest workable design, explicitly defers agentic retrieval, vision models and contextual retrieval until tests show need, and every component (reranker, router, rewrite) is justified.

scores.evidence: 1. Doc loading, search, test harness | 2 wk | Right article in the top 5 for ≥ 90% of answerable questions
scores.rationale: Phases have checkable 'done when' gates, the first step (coverage audit) is concrete, decisions are implementable, and the plan states how it adapts if retrieval or multi-part questions disappoint.

checklist.evidence: Sync on publish events plus a nightly full check. ... The nightly check also removes archived or unpublished articles.
Split articles at H2/H3 headings into chunks of about 200–800 tokens. Never split a numbered procedure or a table.
Build a test set of 200–300 cases from real tickets, with personal data removed
Answer only from the provided docs. If they don't cover the question, say so plainly and offer a human.
The ticket includes the transcript, a two-line summary, what the user wanted, the articles shown and the user's plan
users can plant instructions in them that the model might follow (prompt injection)
Index only public articles, or store the permissions and filter on them. Leaking internal-only articles is the most common failure here.
Mask emails, phone numbers and card numbers before anything is logged, and never store card numbers. Set how long transcripts are kept (e.g. 30–90 days).
Version 1 answers questions from the docs only. It can't look up or change customer accounts.
Each week, review about 50 random conversations plus every thumbs-down, and add the failures to the test set.
each message uses about 5–10k input tokens and about 300 output tokens. That's a few cents per conversation

traps.evidence: Answer only from the provided docs. If they don't cover the question, say so plainly and offer a human.
Index only public articles, or store the permissions and filter on them.
Sync on publish events plus a nightly full check.
Run the tests automatically on every change to prompts, models, chunking or embeddings, and block changes that make scores worse.
Use a fixed pipeline in v1: always retrieve, then answer. It's predictable, cheap and easy to test.

note: An exemplary, proportionate RAG plan that avoids every listed trap and concretely addresses the full checklist; only gaps are the streaming-vs-post-hoc commitment check tension, provider-outage handling, and rollback/incident detail.
